html:
The shipping of Chinese contract labourers to Cuba and Peru from 1847 to 1874, often by fraud or force. Well over 200,000 men made the trip, around 125,000 to Cuba and about 100,000 to Peru.

As Britain pressed to end the African slave trade, sugar planters in Spanish Cuba looked for new workers. Peru wanted labour for sugar estates, railways and the guano islands, where men dug bird droppings for fertiliser. Agents in south China, working out of Macau and treaty ports such as Xiamen, signed men to eight-year contracts. Many were tricked or kidnapped. The Chinese called it the "pig trade".

Conditions on the long voyages were terrible, and many died at sea. In Cuba and Peru the workers were often treated much like slaves and held past their contracts.

In 1874 a Qing commission went to Cuba and took the testimony of thousands of workers. That year Macau banned the trade. Chinese emigration went on elsewhere, as with the miners who went to the gold rushes, and Indian workers went abroad under indenture.
